awd_titl_txt: A Lightning Modeling Grand Challenge Roadmap Workshop; Lubbock, Texas; April 1-3, 2025
awd_abstract_narration:
This grant will support a community conference in 2025 to review and advance a Lightning Modeling Grand Challenge Roadmap. The three-day workshop will include a day of invited talks on components of the grand challenge, followed by a series of breakout discussions to engage the community in refining the roadmap. About 150 attendees are expected.

The conference aims to address the grand challenge of integrating existing knowledge to end-to-end models for either forecast operation or scientific understanding. The conference has three objectives:
1) provide a venue to foster community discussion of the roadmap; 
2) coordinate the efforts of the lightning physics and meteorology community to review scientific hurdles to progress and discuss solutions, updating the roadmap document; 
3) work together in a focused way on pragmatic implementation plans and identification of resources needed to engineer a concrete, interconnected lightning model.

The conference will include a broad cross-section of the lightning physics and lightning meteorology communities, including students and interested participants from university, federal laboratory, industry.  Integrative coordination of the lightning community will mitigate the limitations of siloed progress by smaller groups, as is required to achieve the vision of the Grand Challenge. Development of the lightning model will not only address fundamental science challenges, but will foster new applications of lightning science, new sensor development, and support other agency missions across the nation and world.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Overview:

The goal of this project was to host a three-day community conference in 2025 to discuss and advance a Lightning Modeling Grand Challenge Roadmap. The funding supported the meeting facility at Texas Tech University and attendance of senior and student experts in a workshop format that incorporated input from a broad cross-section of those cognizant in cloud and lightning models, and the underlying physics. Information gathered during the conference - both opportunities and gaps - was summarized and used to guide practical work to advance the Roadmap in the months following the conference, with the aim of building an end to end physical model of cloud processes, lightning, and the sensors that receive lightning signals.


Intellectual Merit:

It remains to be seen whether the observation-driven theories of lightning are self-consistent when asked to make an integrated prediction. This workshop refined plans to connect models of the five major components of an end-to-end lightning model: electrified cloud models, models of the lightning discharge itself, lightning signal propagation, receipt of signals by sensors, and comparison to observations. Attendees of the workshop discussed how this complex, multi-scale problem is at the threshold of being addressable, with theory and computational approaches that are ready to make explicit predictions for comparison to observations. The model and workshop outcomes were summarized in a publication (Behnke et al. 2025, doi:10.1175/BAMS-D-25-0021.1). Following the workshop, various community members have begun to implement preliminary tests of interconnections of the model components. Datasets useful in validating the model were identified and organized on an open version-controlled documentation and source code repository.


Broader impacts:

The workshop fostered a community of practice, with 105 total and 61 in person attendees, including 21 students. Individuals and groups from academia, government, and industry directly interacted on a focused planning task, building working familiarity across the interdisciplinary atmospheric electricity community. Presentations were given at several scientific conferences (in the year after the workshop, and ongoing) describing the end-to-end lightning model and preliminary modeling activities.
